plt.savefig("0.6-0.7_Plot2.png")

Part 6: Estimating the angular scale of the BAO signal¶

In this part, we will use a Python package called iminuit to fit an analytic function to the $\omega(\theta)$. The best fit parameters of our function will allow us to estimate the angular scale of the BAO signal. The iminuit package provides a minimize function that behaves just like the scipy.optimize.minimize function that you learned about in the "Python tools for cosmology and astrophysics" Python skills video. The reason we use it in this activity is that it provides additional, useful tools for calculating the uncertainties on the fitted model parameters.

We already discussed that $\omega(\theta)$ appears to follow a falling power law trend for most of the $\theta$ range, with a small positive deviation (or "bump") around the location of the BAO signal, and some indication of a flattening slope for larger $\theta$ values.

Based on these features, it makes sense to fit the data using a model with two components:

  1. A broken power law component (i.e. a power law that changes slope at a "break"), which we later refer to as the "continuum" model and can be written as \begin{equation} \begin{split} f_\text{BPL}(\theta) = \left \{ \begin{array}{ll} N_\text{BPL}\cdot(\theta / \theta_\text{break}) ^ {-\alpha_1} & : \theta < \theta_\text{break} \\ N_\text{BPL}\cdot(\theta / \theta_\text{break}) ^ {-\alpha_2} & : \theta \ge \theta_\text{break} \\ \end{array} \right. \end{split} \end{equation} This component of our model has four parameters that we can fit:

    1. $N_\text{BPL}$ is a normalisation term that sets the value of $f_\text{PL}$ at $\theta=\theta_\text{break}$.
    2. $\theta_\text{break}$ is the value of theta at which the power-law slope changes (or "breaks").
    3. $\alpha_{1}$ is the power law index that corresponds to the gradient of the power law for $\theta < \theta_\text{break}$, in logarithmic space.
    4. $\alpha_{2}$ is the power law index that corresponds to the gradient of the power law for $\theta > \theta_\text{break}$, in logarithmic space.

    We do not intend to interpret the best fitting parameters of this component physically. It needs to be flexible enough to model the background onto which the BAO signal is superimposed, but simple enough that we can constrain it using the data we have available.

  2. A gaussian component that models the shape of the BAO signal (i.e., the bump): \begin{equation} f_\text{BAO}(\theta)=N_\text{BAO}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{\theta - \theta_\text{BAO}}{\sigma_{BAO}}\right)^{2}\right] \end{equation} This component has three parameters that we can fit:

    1. $N_\text{BAO}$ is a normalisation term that determines the area of the gaussian model for the BAO feature.
    2. $\theta_\text{BAO}$ represents the mean of the gaussian which corresponds with the angular scale of the BAO signal. This is the parameter that we want to measure!
    3. $\sigma_{BAO}$ represents the standard deviation of the gaussian component, which corresponds with the width of the BAO signal feature.

Our combined model will just be the sum of these two components: \begin{equation} f_\text{combined}(\theta, \Theta) = f_\text{BPL}(\theta) + f_\text{BAO}(\theta) \end{equation} where capital theta ($\Theta$) represents a vector containing the seven parameters of our combined model that we need to fit using our data.

Part 6.1 - Implementing our combined model function $f_\text{combined}$¶

Now let's write some Python code that calculates $f_\text{combined}(\theta, \Theta)$ when given one or more values for $\theta$. We will write three functions:

  1. A function called bkn_powerlaw that computes an array of $f_\text{BPL}(\theta)$ values, when given scalar values for $N_\text{BPL}$, $\alpha_1$, $\alpha_2$, $\theta_\text{break}$ and an array of $\theta$ values.
  2. A function called gaussian that computes an array of $f_\text{BAO}(\theta)$, when given scalar values for $N_\text{BAO}$, $\theta_\text{BAO}$, $\sigma_{BAO}$ and an array of $\theta$.
  3. A function called model that receives an array of $\theta$ values and the full parameter array, $\Theta$. The function will extract the individual parameter values, pass appropriate subsets of those values along with the $\theta$ array to the bkn_powerlaw and gaussian functions, and finally return the sum of the arrays of values that bkn_powerlaw and gaussian return. This function serves the same purpose as the function called "model_function" in the Python toolkit notebook example of model fitting.

All of these functions are defined in the next cell. We have added comments to the code to help you understand what it is doing. Please read them carefully, particularly for the model function.

In [45]:
# Function to compute the broken power law component
def bkn_powerlaw(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    norm,  # power law normalisation
    index_below,  # power law index below the break
    index_above,  # power law index above the break
    theta_break,  # angular separation at which the power law breaks
):
    # compute and return the values of the broken power law component using
    # the numpy.where function
    return np.where(
        # A boolean array True at positions where theta < theta_break
        # and False otherwise
        theta < theta_break,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is True i.e. for values of theta below
        # theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_below,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is False i.e. for values of theta above
        # or equal to theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_above,
    )


# Function to compute the gaussian component
def gaussian(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    mean,  # gaussian mean
    sigma,  # gaussian sigma (standard deviation)
    norm,  # gaussian normalisation
):
    # compute and return the values of the gaussian component
    return norm * np.exp(-(((theta - mean) / sigma) ** 2))


# Function to compute the combined model
def model(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    model_params,  # array of all 5 model parameters
):
    # extract the individual model parameters.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    (
        bao_norm,
        bao_location,
        bao_sigma,
        pl_index_1,
        pl_index_2,
        pl_norm,
        pl_break,
    ) = model_params

    # compute the values of the power law components and store the results
    # power_law_1 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_1, pl_index_1)
    # power_law_2 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_2, pl_index_2)
    broken_powerlaw = bkn_powerlaw(theta, pl_norm, pl_index_1, pl_index_2, pl_break)
    # compute the values of the gaussian component and store the result
    bao_signal = gaussian(theta, bao_location, bao_sigma, bao_norm)

    # compute the combined model values by summing the two component arrays
    model = broken_powerlaw + bao_signal

    # return the combined model values
    return model

Part 6.2 - Fitting the model to the measured $\omega(\theta)$ values¶

Now that we have defined our model function we can use the iminuit.minimize function to fit the model to our data. Run the next cell to import the iminuit package and give it the short alias imin.

In [46]:
import iminuit as imin

To use the iminuit.minimize function we need to write one more function. This function will accept a trial set of model parameters, our measured $\omega(\theta)$ values and the values of $\theta$ at which they were measured. The function needs to compute and return a quantity that is guaranteed to be smaller for trial parameters that produce a model that fits the data better - this function will serve the same purpose as the function called "fit_function" in the Python toolkit model fitting example.

One quantity that has this property may be familiar to you. It is called the Chi-Square ($\chi^{2}$) statistic, it is a function of the model parameters ($\Theta$) and can be written mathematically as: \begin{equation} \chi^{2}(\Theta, \theta) = \sum_{\theta}\left(\frac{\omega(\theta) - f(\theta, \Theta)}{\sigma_{\omega}(\theta)}\right)^{2} \end{equation} where $\sigma_{\omega}^{2}(\theta)$ represents the variance associated with $\omega(\theta)$.

In the next cell, we define our fit function to compute the $\chi^{2}$ statistic given a set of model parameters $\Theta$ and a two-dimensional array containing measured values for $\theta$, $\omega(\theta)$ and $\sigma_{\omega}(\theta)$.

We have added comments to the code to help you understand what it is doing. Please read them carefully.

In [47]:
# Fit function that computes the chi-square statistic
def fit_function(model_params, *data):
    # unpack the 2-dimensional data array into three separate data arrays.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    theta, omega, omega_errors = data

    # call the model function to compute values of the combined model
    # given an array of theta values and the set of model parameters
    # that was passed to this function.
    model_omega = model(theta, model_params)

    # compute the chi-square statistic
    chi_square = (((omega - model_omega) / omega_errors) ** 2).sum()

    # return the computed chi_square statistic
    return chi_square

Now that we have defined a function that is guaranteed to return a smaller value for trial parameters that produce a model that fits the data better, we can use the iminuit.minimize function to search for a set of model parameters that produce the smallest possible $\chi^{2}$ value, given our measured data.

We need to provide five arguments to the minimize function. The first three are the same as in the Python toolkit example for scipy.optimize.

  1. The first argument is just the identifier of the function that we want to minimize the output for. For us, this is the fit_function function that we just defined. Notice that we just pass the identifier of the function without any parentheses i.e () and we don't need to create a string by wrapping the identifier in " characters.
  2. The second argument is called x0 and it should be a Python list containing seven elements that represent initial guesses for the model parameters. It is important that these elements are in the order that is expected by our model function when it unpacks them. If you don't remember this order, go back and look again at the code and comments in our definition of the model function.
  3. The third argument that we will pass is called args. We use args to pass a list containing our data arrays. These arrays should be in the order that is expected by our fit_function function when it unpacks them. If you don't remember this order, go back and look again at the code and comments in our definition of the fit_function function.
  4. The fourth argument that we will pass is called bounds. This is a list containing 7 two-element lists, which can be used to nudge the fitting function to find a good result by telling it only to look within a certain range of values for each parameter. In each of the 7 two-element lists the zeroth and first elements represent the minimum and maximum values (or "bounds") that a model parameter can have. The bounds for each parameter should be listed at the same position in the bounds array that the initial guess for that parameter's value appears in the x0 array. Restricting the range of parameter values in this way can help the minimize function to find a best fit solution that makes physical sense.
  5. The final argument is called options. We pass a Python dict containing extra arguments that are used to fine tune the operation of the minimize function. You don't need to understand what these extra arguments mean and you should not need to modify them. We have found that they almost always result in the minimizer converging to a good solution.

Now that we understand what inputs the minimize function requires, we can see that we still need to define some values to proivde as the x0 and bounds arguments.

Let's start with x0 and set up some initial guesses for each of the model parameters. To do this, we need to inspect our plots of $\omega(\theta)$ and consider the descriptions of each of the model parameters at the beginning of this part of the activity (go back and read them if you have forgotten exactly what the parameters mean).

Later in this activity you will be asked to repeat this step for values of $\omega(\theta)$ calculated using galaxies in a different redshift range. At that point you may need to adjust your initial guesses, especially if the data you are trying to fit looks very different.

Run the code in the next cell to set up an array called initial_parameter_guesses that contains appropriate values for this example. Compare the guesses with the plot of $\omega(\theta)$ and try to convince yourself that the guesses make sense. You are free to choose some different initial guesses, but be careful! If you pick values that are too far from the best fitting set to start from, the fitter may not converge properly on the right solution.

In [48]:
# final guesses for parameters
bao_norm = 1.0e-5    # normalisation of the gaussian BAO signal component
bao_location = 2.5  # mean of the gaussian BAO signal component
bao_sigma = 1.1     # sigma of the gaussian BAO signal component
pl_index_1 = -1.85  # index of the broken power law component below the break
pl_index_2 = -1.85  # index of the broken power law component above the break
pl_norm = 0.9e-3    # normalisation of the broken power law component
pl_break = 3.8      # value of theta at which the power law breaks


# collect the initial parameter guesses together into a numpy array in the
# order that is expected by our `model` function.
initial_parameter_guesses = np.array(
    [bao_norm, bao_location, bao_sigma, pl_index_1, pl_index_2, pl_norm, pl_break]
)

To check whether our parameter guesses produce an initial model that fits the calculated $\omega(\theta)$ points reasonably well, let's plot the initial model and data on the same set of axes. The next cell plots:

  1. The rebinned correlation function and its associated errors.
  2. The full model corresponding with our initial paramter value guesses.
  3. The broken power law continuum component of our model corresponding with our initial paramter value guesses.

Run the next cell to generate the plot.

In [49]:
# Create a figure
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 7))

# Create a set of axes attached to our figure
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 1, 1)

# Use the errorbar() method to plot the data
ax.errorbar(
    theta_rebinned,  # The array of rebinned theta values
    omega_rebinned,  # The array of rebinned omega values
    yerr=np.sqrt(omega_var_rebinned),  # The square root of the rebinned variance values
    linestyle="none",  # Don't draw a line between the points on our plot
    marker="o",  # Use a circular marker style
    markersize=3,  # Set a marker size slightly smaller than the default (which is 5)
    label="Measured data",  # Add a label that will be shown in the legend for this plot
)

# Use the `numpy.linspace` function to define a range of theta
# values at which to compute the values of the best fitting model
# function
theta_grid = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 50)

# Now call the `model` function to compute the model values for
# the values of theta in `theta_grid`. Note that we pass an array
# containing the initial parameter values as the second argument
# to the `model` function
initial_model_values = model(
    theta_grid,
    initial_parameter_guesses,
)

# Use the `plot` method of our axes object to plot the initial model
ax.plot(
    theta_grid,  # values of theta to plot the initial model for
    initial_model_values,  # values of the initial model
    label="Initial model",  # Add a label that will be shown in the legend for this plot
)

# Now call the `bkn_powerlaw` function to compute values for the
# broken power law continuum component of our model for the
# values of theta in `theta_grid`. Note that becuse of the way
# we defined the `bkn_powerlaw` function we must pass the parameters
# of our model that pertain to the broken
# power law separately.
initial_continuum_values = bkn_powerlaw(
    theta_grid,  # values of theta to plot the initial model for
    pl_norm,  # the brokemn power law normalisation
    pl_index_1,  # index of the broken power law component below the break
    pl_index_2,  # index of the broken power law component above the break

# Function to compute the broken power law component
def bkn_powerlaw(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    norm,  # power law normalisation
    index_below,  # power law index below the break
    index_above,  # power law index above the break
    theta_break,  # angular separation at which the power law breaks
):
    # compute and return the values of the broken power law component using
    # the numpy.where function
    return np.where(
        # A boolean array True at positions where theta < theta_break
        # and False otherwise
        theta < theta_break,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is True i.e. for values of theta below
        # theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_below,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is False i.e. for values of theta above
        # or equal to theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_above,
    )


# Function to compute the gaussian component
def gaussian(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    mean,  # gaussian mean
    sigma,  # gaussian sigma (standard deviation)
    norm,  # gaussian normalisation
):
    # compute and return the values of the gaussian component
    return norm * np.exp(-(((theta - mean) / sigma) ** 2))


# Function to compute the combined model
def model(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    model_params,  # array of all 5 model parameters
):
    # extract the individual model parameters.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    (
        bao_norm,
        bao_location,
        bao_sigma,
        pl_index_1,
        pl_index_2,
        pl_norm,
        pl_break,
    ) = model_params

    # compute the values of the power law components and store the results
    # power_law_1 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_1, pl_index_1)
    # power_law_2 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_2, pl_index_2)
    broken_powerlaw = bkn_powerlaw(theta, pl_norm, pl_index_1, pl_index_2, pl_break)
    # compute the values of the gaussian component and store the result
    bao_signal = gaussian(theta, bao_location, bao_sigma, bao_norm)

    # compute the combined model values by summing the two component arrays
    model = broken_powerlaw + bao_signal

    # return the combined model values
    return model
In [60]:
# Fit function that computes the chi-square statistic
def fit_function(model_params, *data):
    # unpack the 2-dimensional data array into three separate data arrays.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    theta, omega, omega_errors = data

    # call the model function to compute values of the combined model
    # given an array of theta values and the set of model parameters
    # that was passed to this function.
    model_omega = model(theta, model_params)

    # compute the chi-square statistic
    chi_square = (((omega - model_omega) / omega_errors) ** 2).sum()

    # return the computed chi_square statistic
    return chi_square

def fit_function(model_params, *data):
    # unpack the 2-dimensional data array into three separate data arrays.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will

    # call the model function to compute values of the combined model
    # given an array of theta values and the set of model parameters
    # that was passed to this function.
    model_omega = model(theta, model_params)

    # compute the chi-square statistic
    chi_square = (((omega - model_omega) / omega_errors) ** 2).sum()

    # return the computed chi_square statistic
    return chi_square

# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.

# bounds on mean of the gaussian BAO signal component

# bounds on sigma of the gaussian BAO signal component

# bounds on index of the broken power law component below the break
# Note that we restrict this to be negative, implying a falling power
# law.

# bounds on index of the broken power law component above the break
# Note that we allow this to be slightly positive.

# bounds on normalisation of the broken power law component
# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.
pl_norm_bounds = [1e-4, None]
# bounds on value of theta at which the power law breaks
# Note that we allow a large range of values because we do
# not need the continuum model to be physically meaningful
# but we do need it to be flexible.
pl_break_bounds = [2, 7]

# collect the parameter bounds together into a numpy array in the
# order that is expected by our `model` function.

    [
        bao_norm_bounds,
        bao_location_bounds,
        bao_sigma_bounds,
        pl_index_1_bounds,
        pl_index_2_bounds,
        pl_norm_bounds,

def rebin(theta, omega, omega_variance, points_to_combine=5):
    rebinned = np.array(
        [
            [
                theta[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega_variance[start : start + points_to_combine].sum()
                / points_to_combine**2,
            ]
            for start in range(0, dd.rnom.size, points_to_combine)
        ]
    ).T
    return rebinned

# Function to compute the broken power law component
def bkn_powerlaw(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    norm,  # power law normalisation
    index_below,  # power law index below the break
    index_above,  # power law index above the break
    theta_break,  # angular separation at which the power law breaks
):
    # compute and return the values of the broken power law component using
    # the numpy.where function
    return np.where(
        # A boolean array True at positions where theta < theta_break
        # and False otherwise
        theta < theta_break,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is True i.e. for values of theta below
        # theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_below,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is False i.e. for values of theta above
        # or equal to theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_above,
    )


# Function to compute the gaussian component
def gaussian(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    mean,  # gaussian mean
    sigma,  # gaussian sigma (standard deviation)
    norm,  # gaussian normalisation
):
    # compute and return the values of the gaussian component
    return norm * np.exp(-(((theta - mean) / sigma) ** 2))


# Function to compute the combined model
def model(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    model_params,  # array of all 5 model parameters
):
    # extract the individual model parameters.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    (
        bao_norm,
        bao_location,
        bao_sigma,
        pl_index_1,
        pl_index_2,
        pl_norm,
        pl_break,
    ) = model_params

    # compute the values of the power law components and store the results
    # power_law_1 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_1, pl_index_1)
    # power_law_2 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_2, pl_index_2)
    broken_powerlaw = bkn_powerlaw(theta, pl_norm, pl_index_1, pl_index_2, pl_break)
    # compute the values of the gaussian component and store the result
    bao_signal = gaussian(theta, bao_location, bao_sigma, bao_norm)

    # compute the combined model values by summing the two component arrays
    model = broken_powerlaw + bao_signal

    # return the combined model values
    return model
In [109]:
# Fit function that computes the chi-square statistic
def fit_function(model_params, *data):
    # unpack the 2-dimensional data array into three separate data arrays.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    theta, omega, omega_errors = data

    # call the model function to compute values of the combined model
    # given an array of theta values and the set of model parameters
    # that was passed to this function.
    model_omega = model(theta, model_params)

    # compute the chi-square statistic
    chi_square = (((omega - model_omega) / omega_errors) ** 2).sum()

    # return the computed chi_square statistic
    return chi_square

# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.

# bounds on mean of the gaussian BAO signal component

# bounds on sigma of the gaussian BAO signal component
bao_sigma_bounds = [0.4, 0.9]
# bounds on index of the broken power law component below the break
# Note that we restrict this to be negative, implying a falling power
# law.
pl_index_1_bounds = [-5, -1]
# bounds on index of the broken power law component above the break
# Note that we allow this to be slightly positive.
pl_index_2_bounds = [-3, 0.5]
# bounds on normalisation of the broken power law component
# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.
pl_norm_bounds = [1e-4, None]
# bounds on value of theta at which the power law breaks
# Note that we allow a large range of values because we do
# not need the continuum model to be physically meaningful
# but we do need it to be flexible.
pl_break_bounds = [3, 6]

# collect the parameter bounds together into a numpy array in the
# order that is expected by our `model` function.

    [
        bao_norm_bounds,
        bao_location_bounds,
        bao_sigma_bounds,
        pl_index_1_bounds,
        pl_index_2_bounds,
        pl_norm_bounds,
        pl_break_bounds,
    ]
)

def rebin(theta, omega, omega_variance, points_to_combine=5):
    rebinned = np.array(
        [
            [
                theta[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega_variance[start : start + points_to_combine].sum()
                / points_to_combine**2,
            ]
            for start in range(0, dd.rnom.size, points_to_combine)
        ]
    ).T
    return rebinned

# Function to compute the broken power law component
def bkn_powerlaw(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    norm,  # power law normalisation
    index_below,  # power law index below the break
    index_above,  # power law index above the break
    theta_break,  # angular separation at which the power law breaks
):
    # compute and return the values of the broken power law component using
    # the numpy.where function
    return np.where(
        # A boolean array True at positions where theta < theta_break
        # and False otherwise
        theta < theta_break,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is True i.e. for values of theta below
        # theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_below,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is False i.e. for values of theta above
        # or equal to theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_above,
    )


# Function to compute the gaussian component
def gaussian(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    mean,  # gaussian mean
    sigma,  # gaussian sigma (standard deviation)
    norm,  # gaussian normalisation
):
    # compute and return the values of the gaussian component
    return norm * np.exp(-(((theta - mean) / sigma) ** 2))


# Function to compute the combined model
def model(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    model_params,  # array of all 5 model parameters
):
    # extract the individual model parameters.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    (
        bao_norm,
        bao_location,
        bao_sigma,
        pl_index_1,
        pl_index_2,
        pl_norm,
        pl_break,
    ) = model_params

    # compute the values of the power law components and store the results
    # power_law_1 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_1, pl_index_1)
    # power_law_2 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_2, pl_index_2)
    broken_powerlaw = bkn_powerlaw(theta, pl_norm, pl_index_1, pl_index_2, pl_break)
    # compute the values of the gaussian component and store the result
    bao_signal = gaussian(theta, bao_location, bao_sigma, bao_norm)

    # compute the combined model values by summing the two component arrays
    model = broken_powerlaw + bao_signal

    # return the combined model values
    return model
In [143]:
# Fit function that computes the chi-square statistic
def fit_function(model_params, *data):
    # unpack the 2-dimensional data array into three separate data arrays.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    theta, omega, omega_errors = data

    # call the model function to compute values of the combined model
    # given an array of theta values and the set of model parameters
    # that was passed to this function.
    model_omega = model(theta, model_params)

    # compute the chi-square statistic
    chi_square = (((omega - model_omega) / omega_errors) ** 2).sum()

    # return the computed chi_square statistic
    return chi_square

# Bounds for model parameter values

# bounds on normalisation of the gaussian BAO signal component
# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.
bao_norm_bounds = [1e-3, None]
# bounds on mean of the gaussian BAO signal component
bao_location_bounds = [1.5, 4]
# bounds on sigma of the gaussian BAO signal component
bao_sigma_bounds = [0.4, 0.9]
# bounds on index of the broken power law component below the break
# Note that we restrict this to be negative, implying a falling power
# law.
pl_index_1_bounds = [-5, -1]
# bounds on index of the broken power law component above the break
# Note that we allow this to be slightly positive.
pl_index_2_bounds = [-3, 0.5]
# bounds on normalisation of the broken power law component
# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.
pl_norm_bounds = [1e-4, None]
# bounds on value of theta at which the power law breaks
# Note that we allow a large range of values because we do
# not need the continuum model to be physically meaningful
# but we do need it to be flexible.
pl_break_bounds = [3, 6]

# collect the parameter bounds together into a numpy array in the
# order that is expected by our `model` function.
parameter_bounds = np.array(
    [
        bao_norm_bounds,
        bao_location_bounds,
        bao_sigma_bounds,
        pl_index_1_bounds,
        pl_index_2_bounds,
        pl_norm_bounds,
        pl_break_bounds,
    ]
)

def rebin(theta, omega, omega_variance, points_to_combine=5):
    rebinned = np.array(
        [
            [
                theta[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega_variance[start : start + points_to_combine].sum()
                / points_to_combine**2,
            ]
            for start in range(0, dd.rnom.size, points_to_combine)
        ]
    ).T
    return rebinned

# Function to compute the broken power law component
def bkn_powerlaw(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    norm,  # power law normalisation
    index_below,  # power law index below the break
    index_above,  # power law index above the break
    theta_break,  # angular separation at which the power law breaks
):
    # compute and return the values of the broken power law component using
    # the numpy.where function
    return np.where(
        # A boolean array True at positions where theta < theta_break
        # and False otherwise
        theta < theta_break,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is True i.e. for values of theta below
        # theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_below,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is False i.e. for values of theta above
        # or equal to theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_above,
    )


# Function to compute the gaussian component
def gaussian(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    mean,  # gaussian mean
    sigma,  # gaussian sigma (standard deviation)
    norm,  # gaussian normalisation
):
    # compute and return the values of the gaussian component
    return norm * np.exp(-(((theta - mean) / sigma) ** 2))

# Function to compute the combined model
def model(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    model_params,  # array of all 5 model parameters
):
    # extract the individual model parameters.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    (
        bao_norm,
        bao_location,
        bao_sigma,
        pl_index_1,
        pl_index_2,
        pl_norm,
        pl_break,
    ) = model_params

    # compute the values of the power law components and store the results
    # power_law_1 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_1, pl_index_1)
    # power_law_2 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_2, pl_index_2)
    broken_powerlaw = bkn_powerlaw(theta, pl_norm, pl_index_1, pl_index_2, pl_break)
    # compute the values of the gaussian component and store the result
    bao_signal = gaussian(theta, bao_location, bao_sigma, bao_norm)

    # compute the combined model values by summing the two component arrays
    model = broken_powerlaw + bao_signal

    # return the combined model values
    return model
In [177]:
# Fit function that computes the chi-square statistic
def fit_function(model_params, *data):
    # unpack the 2-dimensional data array into three separate data arrays.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    theta, omega, omega_errors = data

    # call the model function to compute values of the combined model
    # given an array of theta values and the set of model parameters
    # that was passed to this function.
    model_omega = model(theta, model_params)

    # compute the chi-square statistic
    chi_square = (((omega - model_omega) / omega_errors) ** 2).sum()

    # return the computed chi_square statistic
    return chi_square

# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.

# bounds on mean of the gaussian BAO signal component

# bounds on sigma of the gaussian BAO signal component

# bounds on index of the broken power law component below the break
# Note that we restrict this to be negative, implying a falling power
# law.

# bounds on index of the broken power law component above the break
# Note that we allow this to be slightly positive.
pl_index_2_bounds = [-5, 1]
# bounds on normalisation of the broken power law component
# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.
pl_norm_bounds = [1e-4, None]
# bounds on value of theta at which the power law breaks
# Note that we allow a large range of values because we do
# not need the continuum model to be physically meaningful
# but we do need it to be flexible.
pl_break_bounds = [2, 7]


# collect the parameter bounds together into a numpy array in the
# order that is expected by our `model` function.

    [
        bao_norm_bounds,
        bao_location_bounds,
        bao_sigma_bounds,
        pl_index_1_bounds,
        pl_index_2_bounds,
        pl_norm_bounds,

def rebin(theta, omega, omega_variance, points_to_combine=5):
    rebinned = np.array(
        [
            [
                theta[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega_variance[start : start + points_to_combine].sum()
                / points_to_combine**2,
            ]
            for start in range(0, dd.rnom.size, points_to_combine)
        ]
    ).T
    return rebinned

# Function to compute the broken power law component
def bkn_powerlaw(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    norm,  # power law normalisation
    index_below,  # power law index below the break
    index_above,  # power law index above the break
    theta_break,  # angular separation at which the power law breaks
):
    # compute and return the values of the broken power law component using
    # the numpy.where function
    return np.where(
        # A boolean array True at positions where theta < theta_break
        # and False otherwise
        theta < theta_break,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is True i.e. for values of theta below
        # theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_below,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is False i.e. for values of theta above
        # or equal to theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_above,
    )


# Function to compute the gaussian component
def gaussian(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    mean,  # gaussian mean
    sigma,  # gaussian sigma (standard deviation)
    norm,  # gaussian normalisation
):
    # compute and return the values of the gaussian component
    return norm * np.exp(-(((theta - mean) / sigma) ** 2))

# Function to compute the combined model
def model(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    model_params,  # array of all 5 model parameters
):
    # extract the individual model parameters.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    (
        bao_norm,
        bao_location,
        bao_sigma,
        pl_index_1,
        pl_index_2,
        pl_norm,
        pl_break,
    ) = model_params

    # compute the values of the power law components and store the results
    # power_law_1 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_1, pl_index_1)
    # power_law_2 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_2, pl_index_2)
    broken_powerlaw = bkn_powerlaw(theta, pl_norm, pl_index_1, pl_index_2, pl_break)
    # compute the values of the gaussian component and store the result
    bao_signal = gaussian(theta, bao_location, bao_sigma, bao_norm)

    # compute the combined model values by summing the two component arrays
    model = broken_powerlaw + bao_signal

    # return the combined model values
    return model
In [213]:
# Fit function that computes the chi-square statistic
def fit_function(model_params, *data):
    # unpack the 2-dimensional data array into three separate data arrays.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    theta, omega, omega_errors = data

    # call the model function to compute values of the combined model
    # given an array of theta values and the set of model parameters
    # that was passed to this function.
    model_omega = model(theta, model_params)

    # compute the chi-square statistic
    chi_square = (((omega - model_omega) / omega_errors) ** 2).sum()

    # return the computed chi_square statistic
    return chi_square

# bounds on index of the broken power law component below the break
# Note that we restrict this to be negative, implying a falling power
# law.

# bounds on index of the broken power law component above the break
# Note that we allow this to be slightly positive.

# bounds on normalisation of the broken power law component
# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.
pl_norm_bounds = [1e-4, None]
# bounds on value of theta at which the power law breaks
# Note that we allow a large range of values because we do
# not need the continuum model to be physically meaningful
# but we do need it to be flexible.
pl_break_bounds = [3, 6]

# order that is expected by our `model` function.

    [

        bao_location_bounds,
        bao_sigma_bounds,
        pl_index_1_bounds,
        pl_index_2_bounds,
        pl_norm_bounds,
        pl_break_bounds,

def rebin(theta, omega, omega_variance, points_to_combine=5):
    rebinned = np.array(
        [
            [
                theta[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega[start : start + points_to_combine].mean(),
                omega_variance[start : start + points_to_combine].sum()
                / points_to_combine**2,
            ]
            for start in range(0, dd.rnom.size, points_to_combine)
        ]
    ).T
    return rebinned

# Function to compute the broken power law component
def bkn_powerlaw(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    norm,  # power law normalisation
    index_below,  # power law index below the break
    index_above,  # power law index above the break
    theta_break,  # angular separation at which the power law breaks
):
    # compute and return the values of the broken power law component using
    # the numpy.where function
    return np.where(
        # A boolean array True at positions where theta < theta_break
        # and False otherwise
        theta < theta_break,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is True i.e. for values of theta below
        # theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_below,
        # An array of values to choose if the corresponding element of
        # the first argument is False i.e. for values of theta above
        # or equal to theta_break
        norm * (theta / theta_break) ** index_above,
    )


# Function to compute the gaussian component
def gaussian(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    mean,  # gaussian mean
    sigma,  # gaussian sigma (standard deviation)
    norm,  # gaussian normalisation
):
    # compute and return the values of the gaussian component
    return norm * np.exp(-(((theta - mean) / sigma) ** 2))


# Function to compute the combined model
def model(
    theta,  # numpy array of theta values
    model_params,  # array of all 5 model parameters
):
    # extract the individual model parameters.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    (
        bao_norm,
        bao_location,
        bao_sigma,
        pl_index_1,
        pl_index_2,
        pl_norm,
        pl_break,
    ) = model_params

    # compute the values of the power law components and store the results
    # power_law_1 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_1, pl_index_1)
    # power_law_2 = powerlaw(theta, pl_norm_2, pl_index_2)
    broken_powerlaw = bkn_powerlaw(theta, pl_norm, pl_index_1, pl_index_2, pl_break)
    # compute the values of the gaussian component and store the result
    bao_signal = gaussian(theta, bao_location, bao_sigma, bao_norm)

    # compute the combined model values by summing the two component arrays
    model = broken_powerlaw + bao_signal

    # return the combined model values
    return model
In [249]:
# Fit function that computes the chi-square statistic
def fit_function(model_params, *data):
    # unpack the 2-dimensional data array into three separate data arrays.
    # note that we expect them to be in a specific order and we will
    # need to be aware of this when we use the iminuit.minimize
    # function
    theta, omega, omega_errors = data

    # call the model function to compute values of the combined model
    # given an array of theta values and the set of model parameters
    # that was passed to this function.
    model_omega = model(theta, model_params)

    # compute the chi-square statistic
    chi_square = (((omega - model_omega) / omega_errors) ** 2).sum()

    # return the computed chi_square statistic
    return chi_square

# Bounds for model parameter values

# bounds on normalisation of the gaussian BAO signal component
# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.
bao_norm_bounds = [1e-3, None]
# bounds on mean of the gaussian BAO signal component
bao_location_bounds = [1.5, 4]
# bounds on sigma of the gaussian BAO signal component
bao_sigma_bounds = [0.4, 0.9]
# bounds on index of the broken power law component below the break
# Note that we restrict this to be negative, implying a falling power
# law.
pl_index_1_bounds = [-5, -1]
# bounds on index of the broken power law component above the break
# Note that we allow this to be slightly positive.
pl_index_2_bounds = [-3, 0.5]
# bounds on normalisation of the broken power law component
# Note that we do not place an upper bound on this parameter.
pl_norm_bounds = [1e-4, None]
# bounds on value of theta at which the power law breaks
# Note that we allow a large range of values because we do
# not need the continuum model to be physically meaningful
# but we do need it to be flexible.
pl_break_bounds = [3, 6]

# collect the parameter bounds together into a numpy array in the
# order that is expected by our `model` function.
parameter_bounds = np.array(
    [
        bao_norm_bounds,
        bao_location_bounds,
        bao_sigma_bounds,
        pl_index_1_bounds,
        pl_index_2_bounds,
        pl_norm_bounds,
        pl_break_bounds,
    ]
)

    markersize=3,  # Set a marker size slightly smaller than the default (which is 5)
    label="Continuum-subtracted data",  # Add a label that will be shown in the legend for this plot
)

# Use the `numpy.linspace` function to define a range of theta
# values at which to compute the values of the best fitting model
# function
theta_grid = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 50)

# Use the `plot` method of our axes object to plot the best fitting model
ax.plot(
    theta_grid,  # values of theta to plot the initial model for
    # gaussian model for the BAO signal
    gaussian(
        theta_grid,
        fitted_bao_location,
        fitted_bao_sigma,
        fitted_bao_norm,
    ),
    label="Gaussian BAO model",  # Add a label that will be shown in the legend for this plot
)

# Set the x and y axes' titles
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\omega(\theta)$ rebinned - Continuum Model", fontsize="xx-large")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta$ rebinned / degrees", fontsize="xx-large")

# Add a legend to our axes
ax.legend()

# Tidy up the plot
plt.tight_layout()

plt.savefig("0.95-1.05_Plot5.png")

    color="r",
    linestyle="dashed",
    label="Global best fit BAO angular size",
)

# Add a filled grey region illustrating the range spanned by the fit uncertainties
# associated with the BAO angular size
ax.axvspan(
    fitted_bao_location - fitted_bao_location_err,
    fitted_bao_location + fitted_bao_location_err,
    facecolor="lightgrey",
    label="BAO angular size error band",
)

# Set the x and y axes' titles
ax.set_ylabel("$\chi^{2}_{\min}$", fontsize="xx-large")
